rules.title: Instructions to run a command or paste into a terminal (ClickFix)
rules.why: Modern Fake-CAPTCHA / ClickFix attacks convince you to paste a command into Run or a terminal, which downloads malware with no attachment and no obvious link. No legitimate workflow asks you to paste commands from an email.
rules.advice: Never paste commands from an email into Run, PowerShell, Terminal or a browser console. This is malware delivery.

values: click to verify you are human
open the address bar and paste

negations: never run commands from an email
we will never ask you to run
examples: To verify you are human, press Win+R, paste the command below and hit Enter.
falsePositives: Legitimate developer docs mention PowerShell; this rule targets instructions aimed at a non-technical recipient.

rules.title: Request to install remote-support software
rules.why: Telling a victim to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer or a 'remote session' tool is the standard step in tech-support and refund scams: once connected, the attacker drives the victim's machine.
rules.advice: Never install remote-access tools on the instruction of an unsolicited contact. Hang up and call the company using a number you look up yourself.

values: read out the number on the screen
share the id and password shown

examples: Please install AnyDesk so our technician can fix your computer.
falsePositives: Genuine IT departments sometimes use Quick Assist but announce it through known channels.

rules.title: QR-code lure
rules.why: Moving the payload into a QR code defeats link scanners and hides the destination from the reader. This is 'quishing'.
rules.advice: Do not scan QR codes from email. Type the official address yourself instead.
examples: Scan the QR code to verify your account and restore access.
falsePositives: Event tickets and menus use QR codes legitimately; the risk rises with verify/pay/restore wording.

rules.title: Instruction to enable macros or content
rules.why: Asking you to 'enable content' or 'enable editing' defeats the protection that stops document macros from running, which is the classic malware delivery path.
rules.advice: Never enable macros. If you need the document, ask the sender to send a PDF or a plain document.

values: if the document does not open
if you cannot see the content

examples: If the invoice does not display, click Enable Editing then Enable Content.
falsePositives: Corporate templates sometimes mention protected view; combined with an Office attachment it is meaningful.

rules.title: Password for an attached archive is given in the body
rules.why: Password-protected archives (often containing malware) are sent with the password in the email so that antivirus scanners cannot open them.
rules.advice: Do not open password-protected archives from email. This is a deliberate attempt to defeat security scanning.
examples: Attached is the scanned invoice. The password is 12345 to open the ZIP.
falsePositives: Some businesses legitimately send password-protected scans; still worth scrutiny because it defeats AV.

rules.title: Reply/forward subject with no quoted conversation
rules.why: Attackers fake 'RE:' or 'FW:' to make a fresh email look like part of an existing thread, but often fail to include the quoted history a real reply would have.
rules.advice: A weak signal on its own. Check whether you actually had this conversation.
examples: Subject: RE: Invoice payment - but the body has no quoted earlier mail.
falsePositives: Any genuine reply starts with RE:; this only fires when no quoted history is present (handled in code).
